newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Jochimsen warns of rifts if EMU fudged.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Jochimsen warns of rifts if EMU fudged.

text.p: A senior German central banker on Friday issued a stinging critique of European economic and monetary union (EMU), warning that failure to enforce stability targets could lead to rifts opening throughout Europe.

Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said in a speech that EMU was "lop-sided" because it put monetary policy in the hands of an independent central bank without ensuring national governments meet key fiscal restraints to make the euro stable.
He added the stability pact agreed at the European Union's Amsterdam summit lacked teeth and could not provide decisive support to the goal of creating a stable common currency.
And he warned that both France's new government and Germany might miss the Maastricht treaty's stability targets this year.
"There is a sober verdict steadily gaining ground that France is unwilling and Germany unable, any longer at least, to satisfy the criteria," Jochimsen told an academic audience.

Bonn would find it "difficult" to hit the Maastricht treaty budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, while hitting the national debt ceiling of 60 percent of GDP would be "almost impossible".

Launching the euro with a wide group of countries which do not strictly fulfil Maastricht would undermine the working of the stability pact, which could be "smothered by a group in a spirit of shared wrongdoing."

"It does not take much imagination to conclude that states which fail to observe the criteria now will fail to do so in future," said Jochimsen, who is also central bank president in the Social Democrat-ruled state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
He made the remarks as Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Weigel defied sceptics and assured parliament the criteria would be met and the euro would take place on time.
"There will be no soft euro," Weigel said. "We will not allow a softening of the Maastricht criteria."
Also speaking in parliament, Kohl stressed dangers of delaying the project.

"Anyone who wants to delay the euro's introduction has to know that this could possibly be a permanent postponement," Kohl said. "We cannot afford that...We would be throwing away the future for the next generations."
Jochimsen warned that persistent failure to meet EMU goals would create economic strains, force up unemployment in some regions and increase pressure for jobless workers to migrate.

That in turn would lead to calls for extra subsidies to balance out regional differences, risking EMU sliding into "an ever bigger vortex for transfer payments" than seen even in Germany since unification. Bonn has transferred over a trillion marks to the formerly-communist east since 1990.
Failure to put national budgets and economic policies in order would force the independent European central bank to act to contain any resulting inflation pressures, he said.

"In stability terms this accords monetary policy a highly precarious pioneering role, in which it is susceptible to excessive strain and liable to place substantial constraints on growth and employment," Jochimsen said.

Jochimsen warned that using creative accounting to fulfil EMU's entry criteria would put the single currency on "very shaky foundations, at the very least risking a serious crisis of confidence and the upward pressure on interest rates created by the shift of capital into non-EMU currencies".
He said that starting EMU before Europe has taken steps to cut 11 percent unemployment would be "bordering on folly".

Germany's parliament and constitutional court have insisted on strictly fulfilling EMU criteria, and it is against this standard that Bonn's failed bid to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves should be judged, he said.

"How should one expect to bar other budgetary 'sinners' and creative accountants from participation...if one has tried to purchase one's own boarding ticket by using a one-off book trimming exercise that also disregards the legally guaranteed independence of the central bank?" Jochimsen asked.

Wrapping up his speech, Jochimsen echoed former European Commission President Jacques Delors in calling EMU a social experiment: "Given the unaired tensions and still inadequate political and economic foundations, this may do more harm than good to the continuing process of integration in...Europe."
And, departing from his prepared text, Jochimsen said that could lead "to the potential disaster of disintegration."
-- douglas.busvine@reuters.com (Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150)
